title: A comet's hidden gas
blurb: The same comet in a colour where carbon dioxide glows.
story: Same comet, same three hours, a different SPHEREx detector. Every exposure records a slightly different infrared colour. At most colours here 3I/ATLAS is a faint dot, but near 4.26 µm, where carbon dioxide gas glows, it swells into a huge cloud. In this example the big change is colour, not time: play the Time-lapse and watch the wavelength in the caption.

spectrum.hint: It is about 65 times brighter near 4.25 µm than at the other wavelengths measured here. Carbon dioxide gas glows at 4.26 µm, so that is one possible reason: a hint, not proof. Comets give off this gas when sunlight warms their ice. The wavelengths next to it are raised too, so this is not one bad measurement.

doodles.explain: A fuzzy object with a glow around it that moved 562 arcseconds (91.3 SPHEREx pixels) toward the west in 3.2 hours, about 174 arcseconds per hour, while the stars stayed put. Only bodies inside our Solar System cross the sky that fast: an asteroid, or a comet if it looks fuzzy. This is 3I/ATLAS, a known interstellar comet (JPL Horizons).

source: NASA/IPAC IRSA SPHEREx Level-2 spectral images (collections spherex_dr1, spherex_qr3)
